messages.subject: Prepare a simulation's initial state
parts:
Hi all,

Recently, James Paul raised this question, and I think that it's a very interesting and general topic. Maybe some of you already faced this problem: you want to simulate a system, but you want to populate it first. There are mainly two options: 
  1. To warm up the simulation and discard the transitory. But maybe there is no obvious steady-state, so you may want...
  2. To feed the system at t=0 with some initialisation trajectories and generators, so that you don't need to discard anything.
I would like to know how you solve this issue. It would be great if we could identify a problem-agnostic procedure of doing this (if exists), or at least we could arrange some toy examples in a vignette.

Regards,
--
Iñaki Úcar
http://www.enchufa2.es
@Enchufa2

messages.subject: Re: Prepare a simulation's initial state
parts:
Up to now, when I needed a warmup period I only took this into account in the analysis of the results (and potentially in the runtime).
If w is the warmup time, I simply filtered the monitor's results to exclude everything before w. A nice to have could e.g. be the specification of a warmup time in `run()` which is then taken into account by the `get_mon_` functions.

- B

messages.author: 0f5b7adb7e70bd8b
messages.subject: Re: [simmer-devel] Re: Prepare a simulation's initial state
parts:
2016-11-04 17:49 GMT+01:00 Bart Smeets <bartsm...@gmail.com>:
Up to now, when I needed a warmup period I only took this into account in the analysis of the results (and potentially in the runtime).
If w is the warmup time, I simply filtered the monitor's results to exclude everything before w. A nice to have could e.g. be the specification of a warmup time in `run()` which is then taken into account by the `get_mon_` functions.

I think simmer should *not* filter data for two reasons:
  • If the transitory is complex and needs to be determined statistically, you need to do it by yourself in the analysis phase.
  • If the transitory is straightforward, you can simply filter everything before t=t_0, and that's it: there is no gain in simmer doing so.
It might be some gain if the data saturates your RAM. But if that's the case, the warm-up is probably the smallest of your problems. :D

But turning to the pre-initialisation strategy, there may be systems too dependent on the initial conditions (for instance, reaching very different stationary regimes depending on the initial state), so that you may need to set up these initial conditions maching your particular problem.

I would like to spend time on this issue. At some point... I promise. :D For instance, it would be great if we could identify a simple problem, a specific simulation, exhibiting the behaviour I've described.

--
Iñaki Úcar
http://www.enchufa2.es
@Enchufa2

> work is hugely appreciated.

Thank you! Your feedback is much appreciated too.

> Second - I'm wondering if you got round to creating a initialization method
> for trajectories?

There have been some questions in this regard already. The truth is,
as my last email in this thread states, this is a difficult task
because it highly depends on the scenario. I gave this some thought
and I believe there is no universal solution.

However, there may be ways to make life easier for a user wanting to
do perform some initialisation. An enhacement in this line would be
issue #123 on GitHub [1]. Please, take a look at there; any feedback
would be appreciated.

[1] https://github.com/r-simmer/simmer/issues/123
